newsitem.title: FINLAND: Euro unemployment seen high 15 years - Finnish govt.
newsitem.headline: Euro unemployment seen high 15 years - Finnish govt.

text.p: High unemployment is likely to remain a problem in European Union countries for about 15 years and public authorities cannot spend their way out of it, the Finnish government said in a report on the future of Europe.
"Unemployment will probably remain a problem for 15 years or so," said the report, which the Finnish parliament started to debate on Wednesday.
"Because of public deficits and high tax rates, unemployment cannot be decreased or subsistence problems solved by measures calling for more public expenditure," it said.
"A surge in public debt would increase uncertainty about debt management and ultimately raise interest rates, thus decreasing economic activity," it added.
But the unemployment problem required urgent attention.

"Whether or not Europe succeeds in reducing unemployment will decide the future shape of European society," the report said, adding: "Finland feels that employment policy should be more firmly entrenched in the Treaty on European Union."
"Finland regards the creation of a common European employment strategy as a vital imperative."
The chief problem for EU countries was unemployment among low-skilled workers, the report said.
"Technological advances and competition in the various sectors of European production demand a higher level of competence than most of the jobless can offer," it said.

Finland -- suffering the EU's second highest jobless rate -- was trying to boost employment by basing economic growth on high productivity, but also by creating new jobs in labour-intensive branches of the economy.
"Reforms are being introduced in systems of income transfer, taxation and subsidy schemes with the aim of creating new jobs," the government said.

Generous state transfers to households, especially in Nordic countries, have caused problems. Public sector responsibility has been greater than elsewhere in Europe in basic service provision and maintaining employment, it noted.
"Motivation is a weakness ... since the benefit from active participation or personal risk-taking is minimal," the report said.

A pension-bomb is ticking in Europe as the baby-boomers come of retirement age, Finland noted. The projected trend in age structures in EU member states by 2010 indicated that budget pressures would be specially difficult in 2010-2030.
"With the progressive aging of the population, maintaining the work capacity of the baby boom generation is becoming an urgent imperative all over Europe," the report said.
Demography would pose another employment challenge.

The share of young people and people of working age in Europe would fall distinctly over the next 30 years, while the proportion of people over 60 years old would increase to 30 percent by 2025 from from 19 percent now, the report said.
The number of people of working age in Northern African countries would rise 2-4 percent per year, while the same figure in Turkey, the Caucasus and Central Asia would be 1.5-3 percent.
"Combined with the enormous gap in the standard of living between these areas and Europe, pressures for emigration to Europe ... will remain great," the Finnish government said.
